findings.title: Pinned slots are an ACL bypass any admin can fill with any key (role-0 by rule, role-1 by a subset check)
findings.detail: Section 3 says role-0 pinned keys may be added/removed by any admin, and verifier step 4 only enforces `prev.pinned role-1 entries SUBSET-OF E.pinned` for non-role-1 authors, which blocks removals but not additions (the prose 'carried forward verbatim / only a role-1 author may change the role-1 set' is not what the pseudocode checks). Neither rule ties a pinned id to a known key. Sequence: (1) admin A authors an `acl` epoch adding A's second key K as pinned role 1 (or role 0); it passes (pinned/acl disjoint, subset holds, wraps == readers U pinned). (2) K is a recipient of every future M, never appears in GroupAcl/group_acl (ACL only), and under role 1 is an authorized author ordinary admins cannot remove. (3) Another admin kicks A per 4.1: the client wraps for `readers(head.acl - A) U pinned`, so K is re-wrapped automatically; dek_gen bumps, the kick looks complete, and A keeps reading and authoring via K until the offline backup key intervenes. Secondary: mode is derived from 'any role-0 key present', so a role-0 addition to an E2E group makes replicas accept unsigned sig_kind-0 records and re-legalizes w-without-r, and a role-0 removal (E2E enabled) flips a Mode A group to E2E and breaks every plaintext Get/Put client - one admin, contradicting 'per-group choice at genesis'.
findings.fix: Make pinned a genesis-fixed, role-1-controlled object: (a) non-role-1 author => full pinned list of (id, role) pairs must equal prev.pinned; (b) role-1 author may change it but >= 1 role-1 entry must remain; (c) record the server's operational id (or a mode byte) in genesis so role-0 can only be that id and mode cannot change after epoch 1 except via a role-1 epoch of a dedicated kind; (d) show pinned entries in GroupAcl/Groups; (e) negative tests: admin adds role-1, admin adds foreign role-0, admin demotes role-1 to role-0.

findings.title: The verifier accepts a kick that does not roll the key (acl-kind epoch dropping a recipient)
findings.detail: Nothing in 1.4 links a shrinking recipient set to kind == rekey. Step 5 only requires wraps == readers U pinned of the new epoch; step 8 for `acl` requires same dek_gen/dek_commit. Admin A authors `kind = acl` removing X's read bit with fresh wraps to the smaller set and a fresh proof (A has M). Every verifier, replica and audit consumer records 'X removed in epoch n by A' with dek_gen unchanged, while X still holds M and hence the live DEK for everything written afterwards (stolen DB, bundle export, any ciphertext). Today `revoke_read_and_rotate` forces rotation in the same transaction; the new verifier silently regresses that to 'whatever the client chose'. The ask is literally 'kick out AND roll the key'; the chain must not be able to say kicked without rolled.
findings.fix: Verifier rule: if `recipients(prev) - recipients(E)` is non-empty then E.kind == rekey (so dek_gen == prev+1, body_root != 0). Keep `acl` for additions and w/a edits only. Mode A server also refuses an acl epoch that drops a recipient. Golden negative test: acl epoch removing a reader fails.

findings.title: 'rekey changed M' is unverified: dek_commit != prev is vacuous, M reuse is undetectable, and dek_gen can go backwards via adopt at n > 1
findings.detail: dek_commit = HKDF(kcv, Mc, info = group_id || dek_gen) and rekey requires dek_gen == prev+1, so `dek_commit != prev.dek_commit` (step 8) holds even when M is reused - the check proves nothing. A keyless verifier cannot see M, so a rekey reusing M (fresh r) is accepted, and X, kicked in that epoch but holding M_old, derives DEK_new = HKDF(M_old, group_id || dek_gen+1) itself. No recipient-side `M_new != M_old` check is specified either. Separately, step 2 restricts kind in {genesis, adopt} only for epoch == 1 and step 8's adopt rule is just dek_gen == 1 with no relation to prev: at head n (dek_gen 3) an admin submits n+1 `kind = adopt, dek_gen = 1` wrapping the original M_1 (any admin who read at gen 1 has it); the staged commit accepts dek_gen-1 records, and old gen-1 ciphertext (backups, stolen copies, kicked readers' mirrors) is the live generation again.
findings.fix: (a) Define dek_commit over M and group_id only (keep dek_gen in the DEK derivation) so rekey => commit changes and acl => commit equal are meaningful keyless checks pinned to the real M by any recipient opening it. (b) Every recipient checks M_new != M_old on rekey and alerts. (c) Verifier: E.dek_gen in {prev.dek_gen, prev.dek_gen + 1}; genesis/adopt only at epoch 1. (d) Mode A server compares its decrypted M against the previous at CommitEpoch.

findings.title: RemoveIdentity no longer reaches replicas or the chain; re-registering the same EndpointId silently revives every grant including admin
findings.detail: Today remove_identity_with_rotations deletes the identity row, FK-cascades the ACL rows, and the sync roster (group_acl JOIN identity) shrinks so replicas drop the reader; crypto-design promises 'grants do not carry across a key swap'. In the new design the ACL is in the signed epoch and RemoveIdentity 'cannot and does not rewrite any epoch'. (1) Replica authorization source is contradictory: 6.3 keeps unsigned `acl` 'for display' then runs 'existing rules 1-5', which materialize the ACL from that list - either replicas authorize from the unsigned roster (hostile server still forges replica authorization, defeating chain verification) or from the verified epoch (a registry-removed key keeps reading through every replica until some group admin completes 4.1, unbounded - a regression from today). (2) Revival: Bob (rwa on prod) is removed; prod is tainted; nobody re-keys. Weeks later a service admin AddIdentity's Bob's old key under any name for an unrelated purpose; Bob instantly holds rwa in the chain-derived group_acl, reads via the server in Mode A, and can author epochs; no Grant appears anywhere. With a compromised server, a registry-removed admin can still hand it validly signed epochs that replicas accept - replicas have no door.
findings.fix: (a) Replicas authorize by verified-epoch ACL INTERSECT server roster: the roster may only narrow, never widen; names come from the roster. (b) Server refuses AddIdentity for an EndpointId still present in any head-epoch ACL/pinned unless an explicit --revive flag is passed and audited; Groups.tainted lists unregistered ids. (c) Consider letting the role-0 key author a `revoke`-kind epoch that may only remove ACL entries (monotone shrink) so registry removals are chain-visible and replicas enforce them immediately; a compromised online key then gains only denial.

findings.title: ACL and pinned ids are not required to be registered: pre-provisioned hidden grants that activate on a later AddIdentity
findings.detail: The verifier holds no registry (correct), but the design never says the server checks acl/pinned ids against `identity` at BeginEpoch/CommitEpoch; today `grant` resolves the target via identity_by_name and refuses unknowns. Admin A authors an epoch granting rwa to unregistered key X; it verifies. X cannot pass the door, but (1) decrypts any stolen DB or exported bundle, (2) satisfies the last-admin rule after A removes every human, and (3) the moment a service admin registers X under any name, X has rwa with no Grant in any audit trail. With finding 1 the same key can be planted as a pinned recipient.
findings.fix: At CommitEpoch and bundle import the server rejects epochs whose ACL contains an id absent from `identity` and whose pinned entries are not the recorded operational/backup ids. Document it as server policy layered on the chain (replicas cannot and need not check). Mark groups tainted when a head references an unknown id (migration, restore).

findings.title: 4.4 ordering and the kick rebase let the target plant a successor during its own removal
findings.detail: 4.4 runs 4.1 for every administrable group first and sends RemoveIdentity last, so during the multi-group rekey the target T is still registered and (if admin) can author epochs. The CLI fetches head n of prod and starts re-encrypting; T submits n+1 adding key K as rwa. The CLI's commit gets EpochConflict and per 4.1 step 6 restarts with target = T: it computes head.acl - T on top of n+1, so K survives with rwa and M_new is wrapped to K. RemoveIdentity then removes T; the chain holds K. The same auto-rebase hits a plain admin-vs-admin kick (A kicks B while B adds K).
findings.fix: Send RemoveIdentity first (door denial ends T's ability to submit), then re-key the tainted groups; the taint window is harmless with the door shut. In the client kick loop, on EpochConflict diff the new head against the approved snapshot and refuse to auto-rebase if the intervening epoch was authored by the target or changes anything else; show the diff and require confirmation.

findings.title: A CAS-losing epoch is a valid fork the store can serve to other replicas (equivocation)
findings.detail: Two admins at head n both submit n+1 (A kicks B, B kicks A). CAS picks one, but the loser's epoch is a fully valid signed extension of n that the server received and can retain. A hostile or buggy authoritative node serves A's n+1 to replica R1 and B's n+1 to R2; each verifies, each pins a different head, and R2 keeps serving B. Pins are per-verifier with no cross-check, so it is invisible until heads are compared by hand. 5.2's 'cannot forge ACL changes' is true, but choosing between two legitimately signed alternatives at the same height keeps a kicked admin live on part of the fleet; risk 6 covers rollback, not this.
findings.fix: Server countersigns accepted epochs with its endpoint key (receipt over epoch_hash, height); replicas/clients require it, so two receipts at one height are a portable proof of equivocation. Add a cheap cross-check: the k8s operator exports (group_id, head_epoch, head_hash) as a metric and CLI status compares its pin to the replica it uses. A CAS-losing client keeps the losing epoch and warns if it ever sees it accepted.

findings.title: A rekey is a silent history-rewrite channel with forged origin attribution; the Mode A server decrypts staged records but never compares them
findings.detail: 4.1 replaces every secret_version row with kind-1 records signed by the rekeying admin, with origin_author/origin_at 'attested only by author', and deletes the originals. Admin A can change the plaintext of db-password v4 (current or historical) during a rekey and stamp origin_author = Bob, origin_at = old; every display shows 'v4 by Bob' with A's content, and no new version or Put audit row exists - today a rewrite necessarily creates a new version attributed to the writer. The Mode A server already decrypts every staged record (4.1 step 5) and has DEK_old via its wrap, so comparing plaintexts is nearly free, but the design does not. In Mode B nothing links a kind-1 record to the one it replaced, so even a reader holding the old bundle cannot prove the rewrite from the chain.
findings.fix: Add from_record_hash to SBR1 kind-1 records; verifier/bundle-verify check origin_author/origin_at/name/version equal the referenced record when available, and body_root commits to lineage. Mode A CommitEpoch decrypts each staged record and the current row and rejects on plaintext mismatch (or requires an audited explicit rewrite flag). Keep pre-rekey record hashes in the epoch/bundle so an auditor can detect a replaced lineage after deletion.

findings.title: Any writer can block every future kick by storing an undecryptable record
findings.detail: 4.1 step 3 decrypts every retained version with DEK_old before re-encrypting; an AEAD failure aborts the client's rekey. PutRecord in Mode A is checked only structurally (caller == author, write, dek_gen/epoch current, CAS) - the server does not decrypt it - and in Mode B nobody can. So a write-holder (including a w-only CI key that cannot derive the DEK, or a service admin exercising authorize_group's implicit write on an E2E group, which 5.1 claims is 'gone') submits a validly signed record with garbage ciphertext. From then on no admin can complete 4.1: the kicked reader keeps a live key, and the only remedy is to Delete the poisoned secret. Combined with the fixed 10-minute staging GC and 4 MiB values, a large group can be made un-rekeyable by volume alone.
findings.fix: Mode A: the server decrypts every PutRecord at submit and rejects on AEAD failure, as it does for staged records. Both modes: the rekey client quarantines undecryptable records (it cannot carry them since AAD binds dek_gen) into a signed dropped_records list in the epoch, audited by the server; a kick must never be blocked by data it cannot read. Size staging GC by bytes staged. Explicitly remove the service admin's implicit write/delete on E2E groups.

findings.title: Pins die with a dropped group: withhold, drop, re-present the same name under a new genesis
findings.detail: Pins live in secret_group on the replica and 'a group absent from a completed manifest is dropped locally' (rule 8, drop_group_local cascades everything). The server omits prod from one full manifest; the replica drops it and its pin; the next manifest presents prod with a fresh group_id and a server-authored genesis with any ACL; the replica pins it on first sight and serves it. No signature is forged. Clients pinning by group_id have the same hole when the server rebinds the name. In Mode A the server already reads everything (marginal gain is laundering authorization through replicas); in Mode B the fake chain cannot carry real plaintext, so the impact is denial/confusion - but it falsifies the 'replicas verify chains' claim for any replica that ever lost a group.
findings.fix: Keep pins as tombstones keyed by (server, name) -> (group_id, genesis_hash, head) across drops; refuse a same-name group with a different group_id or genesis unless an operator explicitly resets the pin, and log it as an alarm. Clients do the same.

findings.title: An epoch whose dek_commit does not open bricks Mode B replicas permanently if 'refuse the epoch' means 'do not advance'
findings.detail: 1.5 says a recipient finding a dek_commit mismatch must refuse the epoch. In Mode B the server cannot check the commit at submit, so admin A pushes n+1 with a bogus commit; every replica refuses and stays at n. Chain verification of n+2 depends only on n+1's ACL, so a legitimate admin's or the backup key's n+2 is a valid extension - but a replica that refused n+1 never has a chain to extend and is stuck forever. Break-glass cannot help if replicas will not move past the poisoned epoch.
findings.fix: Separate chain acceptance from decryptability: advance the pin on any epoch that verifies (1.4), record 'undecryptable at epoch n by author', stop serving that group's plaintext, resume at the next decryptable epoch. Never let a decrypt-time check block chain advancement.

findings.title: Migration synthesizes origin_author from the created_by name, attributing old writes to whoever holds the name today
findings.detail: secret_version.created_by is an identity name, and the documented key-replacement procedure is RemoveIdentity + AddIdentity under the same name. 6.4 sets origin_author = the id behind created_by if it still exists, so every historical write by the old holder of 'bob' becomes operational-key-signed attestation that the current 'bob' key wrote it. The chain carries a forged origin forever.
findings.fix: Leave origin_author zero and origin_at = created_at for migrated records; keep created_by display-only. Only post-migration records carry an id-based origin.

findings.title: Records do not chain to the version they supersede, so a pre-signed record from a writer who later lost write can be inserted by whoever writes the store
findings.detail: SBR1 binds (group_id, epoch, dek_gen, name, version) but not the predecessor. Writer W with write at epoch 5 pre-signs (name, version 9, epoch 5, dek_gen 1); W loses write in epoch 6 (acl kind, dek_gen unchanged). Later at current version 8, a DB writer or hostile server inserts W's record as version 9: replicas check dek_gen == head's, epoch 5 exists, W held write at 5 - accepted. Out of the stated threat model (DB write = operator) but cheaply closable, and it bounds the otherwise unfalsifiable 'epoch as authorization context' field.
findings.fix: Add prev_record_hash to SBR1 (0^32 for version 1); replicas/bundle-verify check the link so a version-9 record must name version 8's hash, which did not exist when W had write.

strengths: Authorization is checked against the previous signed epoch, never a server table; the admin bit is enforceable by a keyless verifier (the section 7.2 argument is correct).
admin => read, >= 1 ACL admin, pinned/acl disjointness and the exact recipients == readers U pinned rule are all keyless and cheap.
Role-0 (operational) keys are not authorized authors, so a compromised online key cannot rewrite ACLs; the server authors epoch 1 only.

One live dek_gen with full re-encryption closes today's 'stolen DB + kicked key reads history' gap, and the staged CAS commit on both epoch number and the exact (name, version) set makes a kick atomic.
Mode A's server-side decrypt of its own wrap and every staged record catches a rekey that would brick readers before replicas see it.
Epoch author + signature gives exactly the 'who last re-encrypted' answer the user asked for, and the break-glass bundle round-trip removes the service-stopped db grant / recover paths.
Pins for genesis and head give rollback detection without any server trust.
verdict: The cryptographic core (chain, signature, DLEQ, keyless verify) is sound and the governance shape is right, but the verifier pseudocode is weaker than the prose in four load-bearing places - pinned role sets (any admin can plant a permanent hidden reader/admin), kick without rekey, rekey without a new M (the dek_commit check is vacuous), and non-monotonic dek_gen - and the registry/chain split is unspecified for replicas and for re-registration, which turns RemoveIdentity into a revivable grant. Each is closable with a small verifier rule or server submit check; the design should not ship until findings 1-5 are closed and the kick-flow ordering (6) and history-rewrite gap (8) are addressed.
